props.title: Up Pompeii

sections.content: **Up Pompeii** (1971) epitomizes the bawdy British comedy tradition of the early 1970s, spinning off from the successful BBC television series. Frankie Howerd's portrayal of the slave Lurcio draws directly from the music hall tradition and borrows heavily from the **Carry On** series (1958-1978) style of double entendre and sexual innuendo. The film follows similar territory to A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum (1966), combining ancient Roman settings with vaudevillian humor and slapstick comedy.

sections.content: The film represents a crucial moment in British comedy cinema, bridging the gap between traditional seaside postcard humor and the more sophisticated comedy that would emerge later in the decade. While **Monty Python's Life of Brian** (1979) would later revolutionize historical comedy with sharper satire, Up Pompeii maintains the traditional British comedy elements of innuendo, mistaken identity, and physical comedy that dominated the era's humor.

Director Bob Kellett, who also helmed **Are You Being Served?** (1977), brings a theatrical staging to the film that reflects its television origins. The approach mirrors other British TV-to-film adaptations of the period like **On the Buses** (1971) and **Steptoe and Son** (1972), preserving the familiar elements that made the source material popular while expanding the scope for cinema. sections.content: The film sits within a larger tradition of comedic takes on ancient history, though with distinctly British sensibilities. While Hollywood produced lavish historical epics like **Cleopatra** (1963), British cinema often approached the ancient world through comedy, from Carry On Cleo (1964) to later works like **Yellowbeard** (1983). This approach typically favored broad humor and sexual innuendo over historical accuracy, using ancient settings as a backdrop for contemporary comedy styles.
